title: Getting Around Thai Islands Without a Scooter
content:
Not everyone wants to ride a scooter, and on some Thai islands you do not need to. What varies enormously is what fills the gap — a frequent shared-truck network on one island, a handful of charter taxis at fixed rates on another. This is what the alternatives actually look like, island by island.

What a songthaew is

A songthaew is a pickup truck with a covered bed and two bench seats facing each other. On most Thai islands it functions as the closest thing to public transport. Where a genuine network operates, you flag one down, ride along a broadly fixed route, and pay a set fare when you get out.

The word covers two quite different things, though, and the difference matters. On some islands songthaews behave like shared buses: they run set routes, pick up whoever is going that way, and charge per person. On others the same vehicle operates as a chartered taxi — a fixed price for the whole truck, negotiated or posted, whether you are one passenger or four.

Island by island

Koh Samui

Songthaews circle the ring road, which runs about 51 km around the island and passes through most of the main beach towns. Routes follow driver preference more than a published timetable, but the network is real and continuous during daylight. Fares run roughly 30 to 150 baht depending on distance — a wide band, because a hop between adjacent beach towns and a run across the island are both served by the same trucks. Service thins out in the evening, whereas Grab, which also operates here, does not keep those hours.

Phuket

Fixed routes run from Phuket Town out to the individual beaches, roughly 6am to 6pm, at about 15 to 50 baht — the cheapest fares of any island here. The shape of that network matters more than the price, though: it radiates from the town rather than connecting the beaches to each other, so a trip between two neighbouring beaches often means going in and back out, while the same distance on Koh Samui's ring road is a single ride. Phuket is around 48 to 50 km long. Grab operates, which is the usual way people cover beach-to-beach.

Krabi and Ao Nang

Ao Nang is on the mainland rather than an island, and it has the most conventional service of any of these places: colour-coded fixed routes with flag-down stops, running every 10 to 20 minutes through the day, at 50 to 60 baht. That frequency is the outlier — elsewhere on this page the honest answer to "when does the next one come" is unknown, whereas here it is a number. Krabi Town to Ao Nang is about 17 to 20 km. Grab operates as well.

Koh Lanta

Fixed routes connect the west-coast beaches with Saladan town at the north end, at roughly 50 to 100 baht. The island is long and narrow, around 25 to 30 km, with the beaches strung along one coast. Operating hours are not reliably documented. Grab does not appear to operate.

Koh Phangan

Shared pickup trucks run along the main roads, but fares are frequently negotiated rather than posted, and reported prices vary widely — anywhere from 50 to 500 baht depending on distance and the negotiation. The island is about 16 to 18 km across, with accommodation spread across multiple separate bays. Operating hours are not documented. Grab does not operate.

Koh Chang

Shared trucks run along the west-coast main road and are flagged down; services tend to cluster around ferry arrival times. Fares run roughly 50 to 200 baht. Grab does not operate.

Koh Tao

Koh Tao is the outlier and worth describing carefully. Pickup trucks marked as taxis wait at Mae Haad pier, at the Sairee junction, and near the 7-Eleven in Chalok Baan Kao. They look like songthaews elsewhere. They do not behave like them.

Rates are fixed per route rather than per person: commonly 300 to 500 baht for one or two people from Mae Haad, with about 100 baht added for each additional passenger. Drivers frequently wait to fill the truck before departing, so a solo traveler either pays for the whole vehicle or waits for strangers. The island is small — about 7.5 km long, with the main bays generally under 5 km apart. Set that against Phuket, forty times the length, where the same journey distance costs 15 to 50 baht: the smallest island here has the highest per-trip fares, not the lowest. For two people the per-head cost falls by half; for four it falls again. The fare structure rewards groups and penalises solo travel, which is the reverse of how per-person fares work everywhere else on this page.

Mae Haad and the southern end of Sairee are walkable. The terrain between bays is hilly, and the roads have no footpaths. Grab does not operate.

Where Grab stops

The app-based option follows a clear line. Grab operates in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui and the Krabi and Ao Nang area. It does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan, and appears not to on Koh Lanta or Koh Chang.

That line falls in the same place as several other things. The islands without Grab are generally the ones where the shared-truck network is least formal, where fares are negotiated rather than posted, and where operating hours are least documented. The places with the most transport options have the most of all of them; the places with the fewest have fewer of each.

What is not documented

Two things are worth flagging as genuinely unclear rather than merely unstated. Songthaew operating hours on Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta are not reliably published anywhere — the practical answer is daylight, with the evening cutoff varying. And Koh Phangan's fares are reported so inconsistently across sources that the honest description is a wide band rather than a figure.

Where fares are negotiated rather than posted, the price you are quoted and the price someone else was quoted may differ, and neither is wrong.

How this fits the rest of the trip

The transport picture on any one island is only half of what determines how you move around it. The other half is where the things you came for actually sit — how far the beach is from the town, whether the restaurants cluster in one strip or scatter across separate bays, and how far apart the bays are.

Those distances, and how they interact with each island's transport, are laid out in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

What is a songthaew?

A pickup truck with a covered bed and two bench seats, used as shared transport. On some islands it runs fixed routes and charges per person; on others the same vehicle operates as a chartered taxi at a fixed price for the whole truck.

Does Grab work on the Thai islands?

On some. It operates in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui and the Krabi and Ao Nang area, and does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan. Coverage on Koh Lanta and Koh Chang appears to be absent as well.

How much do songthaews cost?

It varies by island. Phuket runs about 15 to 50 baht, Krabi and Ao Nang 50 to 60, Koh Samui 30 to 150, Koh Lanta 50 to 100. Koh Tao is the outlier, with fixed per-route rates commonly 300 to 500 baht for one or two people.

What time do songthaews stop running?

Phuket runs roughly 6am to 6pm. Elsewhere the honest answer is daylight hours with an evening cutoff that is not reliably documented, particularly on Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta.

Why are Koh Tao's taxi fares so high?

Rates there are fixed per route rather than per person, so a short trip costs the same whether you are one passenger or two. With the island only about 7.5 km long and the main bays under 5 km apart, the fares are high relative to the distances.
excerpt: What fills the gap if you do not ride — songthaew networks, fares and coverage, island by island.

title: How Far Apart Things Are on Thai Islands
content:
How much moving around an island actually involves depends on two things that rarely appear in the same place: how far apart its beaches, towns and restaurants sit, and what it costs to cover that ground. Here are the measurements for the islands Americans most often visit.

Two different kinds of island

The islands split along a line that has nothing to do with size. Some have their beaches, restaurants and accommodation concentrated in one strip, where a single walkable area contains most of what a visitor came for. Others spread the same things around a coastline or across separate bays, with unpopulated road between each cluster.

A large island with a concentrated centre can involve less daily movement than a small island with scattered bays. Koh Tao is under 8 km long and requires more transport than its size suggests; Ao Nang is on the mainland and requires almost none.

The measurements

Phuket

Around 48 to 50 km long, and the most spread out of these places. The beaches run down the west coast, with Phuket Old Town inland to the southeast. The main town sits roughly 10 to 20 km from the beaches depending which one. Patong's beach strip and the Old Town each have walkable centres; the island as a whole does not. Songthaews run town-to-beach rather than beach-to-beach, at 15 to 50 baht, roughly 6am to 6pm. Grab operates.

Koh Samui

The ring road runs about 51 km and passes through most of the main beach towns. Chaweng and Fisherman's Village have walkable centres; the island's attractions are spread around the ring rather than gathered in one place. Songthaews circle the ring during daylight at 30 to 150 baht, without a fixed timetable. Grab operates.

Koh Lanta

About 25 to 30 km, long and narrow, with the beaches strung along the west coast and Saladan town at the north end. The shape is the important part: accommodation at the southern end sits a long way from the town where the ferries arrive and most services cluster. Songthaews connect the beaches to Saladan at 50 to 100 baht. Grab does not appear to operate.

Koh Phangan

Around 16 to 18 km across, with accommodation spread across multiple separate bays rather than one strip. Thong Sala is the main town and ferry arrival point. Haad Rin, at the southern tip, is a separate cluster. Getting between bays means road transport, at fares reported anywhere from 50 to 500 baht. Grab does not operate.

Koh Tao

About 7.5 km long — the smallest here — with the main bays generally under 5 km apart. Mae Haad, Sairee and Chalok Baan Kao are the three main villages, connected by one wide paved road with side roads leading over to the east coast bays.

Mae Haad and the southern part of Sairee are walkable, and the roads have no footpaths. The terrain between bays is hilly. Fixed taxi rates from Mae Haad run about 300 baht to Sairee or Chalok and 400 to 500 to the more distant bays, for one or two people, with roughly 100 baht per additional passenger. Grab does not operate.

Ao Nang and Krabi

Ao Nang is on the mainland, not an island. Its beachfront is concentrated and walkable, with restaurants and shops along one strip. Krabi Town is about 17 to 20 km away, connected by colour-coded songthaews running every 10 to 20 minutes at 50 to 60 baht. Grab operates.

Koh Chang

The accommodation runs along the west coast, spread along the main road rather than gathered in one town. White Sand Beach has a walkable strip. Shared trucks run the coast road at 50 to 200 baht, clustering around ferry arrivals. Grab does not operate.

Roads and darkness

Two physical facts apply nearly everywhere outside Bangkok. Street lighting is poor to absent on island and mountain roads after dark — every region surveyed reports the same thing. And most island roads have no footpaths, so walking between bays means sharing the carriageway with traffic.

Terrain varies more than the flat-beach mental image suggests. Koh Samui has a hilly interior behind its coastal ring road. Phuket is hilly with winding coastal roads. Koh Tao's bays are separated by high ground. Distances measured on a map and distances experienced on the ground diverge accordingly.

What the numbers do not tell you

Two gaps are worth naming. Operating hours for the shared-truck networks on Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta are not reliably documented anywhere — the practical answer is daylight, with an evening cutoff that varies. And Koh Phangan's fares are reported so inconsistently that the honest description is a wide band.

Where this leads

Distances, transport coverage and fare structures are three separate measurements, and they interact in ways that only become visible when you put them beside the specific place you are staying and the specific things you want to reach. An island can be small and still demanding; large and still easy.

How the numbers on this page combine into a picture of a particular trip is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Which Thai islands are walkable?

Ao Nang's beachfront is concentrated and walkable. Koh Tao's Mae Haad and southern Sairee are walkable, though the bays beyond are hilly and up to 5 km apart. Phuket and Koh Samui have walkable pockets — Patong, the Old Town, Chaweng, Fisherman's Village — within islands that are otherwise spread out.

How big is Koh Tao?

About 7.5 km long, with the main bays generally under 5 km apart. Its taxi fares are high relative to those distances.

How far is Krabi Town from Ao Nang?

About 17 to 20 km, with colour-coded songthaews running every 10 to 20 minutes through the day at 50 to 60 baht.

Are Thai island roads lit at night?

Generally not. Street lighting is poor to absent on island and mountain roads outside the urban areas, and most island roads have no footpaths.

Which islands are most spread out?

Phuket at 48 to 50 km is the largest and most dispersed. Koh Lanta is long and narrow at 25 to 30 km with beaches strung along one coast. Koh Phangan spreads accommodation across separate bays despite being only 16 to 18 km across.
excerpt: Real distances between the places visitors go, and what it takes to cover them on each island.

title: Renting a Car in Thailand: Paperwork, Cost and Roads
content:
Renting a car gets far less attention than renting a scooter, and the requirements are meaningfully different. Here is what a car actually involves in Thailand — the paperwork, the cost, the roads it suits, and what the insurance does and does not cover.

What the paperwork requires

Driving a car in Thailand requires a valid home driving licence plus an International Driving Permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention. In the United States, AAA and AATA are the only authorised issuers, at around $20, available same-day in person at a AAA branch.

There is a difference here that catches people who have read about scooters. A car requires the ordinary driving licence an American already holds. A motorbike requires a motorcycle endorsement on that licence, which most Americans do not have, and which an IDP does not add. The permit that covers you for a car may not cover you for a scooter — the entitlement comes from the home licence, and the IDP only translates it.

What it costs

Daily rates run roughly 700 to 1,500 baht depending on class, with economy cars at the lower end and SUVs and pickups higher. That sits well above a day of songthaew trips almost anywhere except Koh Tao, where four fixed-rate taxi runs at 300 to 500 baht each would cost more than a car for the day — if a car were practical on an island that size, which it is not. Rates move with season and demand, so treat any figure as a shape rather than a price:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

What the insurance covers

A standard rental includes compulsory third-party liability, which covers injury or death to other people. It does not cover damage to the rental vehicle itself.

Collision damage waiver and theft protection are separate add-ons, and both carry common exclusions — off-road driving being the usual one. The gap between "insured" as the counter describes it and "insured" as a renter assumes it tends to sit exactly there: third-party injury is covered by default, the car you are driving is not.

Worth reading the specific terms rather than the summary, and worth checking what your own travel insurance says about rental vehicles, since policies differ on whether they duplicate or supplement the rental company's cover.

Where the roads suit a car

Road networks vary enough that the question is less about preference than about physical fit.

The mainland and the north have the road networks best suited to a car. Chiang Mai and the routes north of it are mountainous with sharp curves and switchbacks — Route 1095 to Pai is commonly cited as having 762 curves over about 135 km — but they are proper roads with room for four wheels.

Phuket and Koh Samui both have developed road networks. Samui's ring road runs about 51 km around the island; Phuket is 48 to 50 km long with winding coastal and mountain roads and heavier traffic than the smaller islands.

The smaller islands have narrow roads that do not accommodate cars well. Koh Tao is about 7.5 km long with one main paved road between the villages and side roads over hilly terrain to the east coast bays. Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta are similarly constrained. This is where the paperwork advantage inverts: a car is the easier vehicle to be licensed for and the harder one to actually use, whereas a scooter is the harder one to be licensed for and fits everywhere. The places where the licensing question is most awkward are the places where four wheels are least practical.

Parking

Resorts and shopping centres generally provide parking. The busy beach towns are constrained, and street parking is restricted to legal zones.

Night driving

Street lighting is poor to absent outside Bangkok and the main urban areas. Island and mountain roads are largely unlit after dark, which is the single most consistent road-condition finding across every region. The mountain routes that make a car attractive during the day are the ones with no lighting at night.

How this sits beside the alternatives

A car is one of four ways to cover ground in Thailand, alongside a scooter, the shared-truck networks, and app-based rides where they operate. Each has a different paperwork requirement, a different cost structure, and a different set of places it physically fits.

Which combination suits a particular set of bases and a particular tolerance for driving is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Do I need an International Driving Permit to rent a car in Thailand?

Yes — a valid home licence plus a 1949 Geneva Convention IDP. In the US, AAA and AATA are the only authorised issuers, at around $20, available same day in person.

Is a car easier than a scooter, paperwork-wise?

For most Americans, yes. A car requires the ordinary driving licence you already hold. A motorbike requires a motorcycle endorsement that most US licences lack, and an IDP does not add one.

What does rental car insurance in Thailand cover?

Standard rentals include compulsory third-party liability, covering injury to other people. Damage to the rental vehicle itself is not included — collision damage waiver and theft protection are separate add-ons with common exclusions.

How much does a rental car cost in Thailand?

Roughly 700 to 1,500 baht per day depending on class, though rates move with season and demand.

Where in Thailand do the roads suit a rental car?

The mainland, the north, Phuket and Koh Samui have developed road networks. The smaller islands — Koh Tao, Koh Phangan, Koh Lanta — have narrow roads that accommodate cars poorly.

title: Where Grab Works in Thailand (and Where It Does Not)
content:
Grab is Thailand's dominant ride-hailing app, and where it operates it removes most of the friction of getting around — fixed prices, no negotiation, no language barrier. Where it does not operate, the fallback is a different system with different rules. Here is the actual coverage map.

Where Grab operates

Grab runs in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui, and the Krabi and Ao Nang area. In each of these, both car and motorbike-taxi options are generally available, with the motorbike option cheaper and faster in traffic.

The pricing model is the thing that distinguishes it: you see the fare before you book, and it does not change. No meter to refuse, no negotiation, no route dispute.

Where it does not

Grab does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan. It appears not to operate on Koh Lanta or Koh Chang, though the evidence there is thinner.

The line falls in a consistent place. Grab covers the large developed islands and the mainland cities. It stops at the smaller islands.

What that line coincides with

The islands without Grab share several other characteristics, and they compound rather than offset.

Where Grab operates, the shared-truck networks also tend to be more formal — Phuket runs fixed routes 6am to 6pm at 15 to 50 baht, Ao Nang runs colour-coded routes every 10 to 20 minutes at 50 to 60 baht. Where Grab does not operate, fares are more often negotiated than posted, operating hours are less documented, and the per-trip cost is higher. The two do not offset each other. Somewhere with a good shared-truck network but no Grab would be one thing; somewhere with neither is another. The islands fall into the second group rather than the first.

Koh Tao is the clearest illustration. No Grab, and its pickup-truck taxis charge fixed per-route rates of about 300 to 500 baht for one or two people from Mae Haad, with roughly 100 baht per additional passenger, on an island only 7.5 km long. Koh Phangan has no Grab and fares reported anywhere between 50 and 500 baht depending on distance and negotiation.

So the places with the fewest transport options also have the least price transparency and the highest per-trip cost. The gap is not evenly distributed — and it runs opposite to what island size would suggest, since the small islands people expect to be cheap and simple are the ones where a single trip costs the most and the price is least knowable in advance. On Phuket or Samui the choice is between several priced options; on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan it is between one unpriced option and your own two wheels.

The metered alternative in the cities

In Bangkok and Chiang Mai, metered taxis operate alongside Grab. The meter exists and is legally required to be used. Whether a given driver uses it is a separate matter, which is covered in our guide to tuk-tuks and taxis in Thailand.

The practical difference is that Grab's price is agreed before the ride and a taxi's is settled after it. That distinction matters more where you do not speak the language or know the route.

What is not well documented

Wait times are the main gap. There is no reliable figure for how long a Grab typically takes to arrive in any of the places it operates, and reported experiences vary with time of day and location within each place.

Coverage on Koh Lanta and Koh Chang is also less certain than the clear absence on Koh Tao and Koh Phangan — the evidence points to no service, but it rests on fewer sources.

How coverage interacts with everything else

Ride-hailing availability is one layer of a picture that also includes how far apart things sit on each island, what the shared-truck networks cost and when they run, and what the road conditions are like after dark. Each of those is documented separately and none of them alone describes what a day of moving around actually looks like.

How the layers combine for a specific set of bases is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Does Grab work in Thailand?

In Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui and the Krabi and Ao Nang area. It does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan, and appears not to on Koh Lanta or Koh Chang.

What do I use where Grab does not operate?

The local shared pickup trucks, which on those islands tend to run as fixed-rate charter taxis rather than shared routes. On Koh Tao that means about 300 to 500 baht per trip for one or two people.

Is Grab cheaper than a taxi in Bangkok?

Not necessarily cheaper, but the price is fixed and shown before you book, which removes the meter question entirely.

Does Grab offer motorbike taxis?

Yes, in the areas where it operates. The motorbike option is cheaper than the car option and faster in heavy traffic.

How long do Grab rides take to arrive?

There is no reliable published figure. Reported wait times vary considerably by time of day and by location within each area it serves.

title: Thai Road Conditions by Region
content:
Thailand's roads vary more than the flat-beach mental picture suggests, and the differences are physical rather than a matter of confidence. Here is what the surfaces, gradients, traffic and lighting are actually like, region by region.

The one thing that applies almost everywhere

Street lighting is poor to absent outside Bangkok and the main urban areas. Island roads, mountain roads and rural stretches are largely unlit after dark. This is the most consistent finding across every region surveyed, and it applies equally to a car, a scooter and someone walking.

Most island roads also have no footpaths. Walking between bays means sharing the carriageway with traffic, which is a daylight consideration and a considerably larger one after sunset.

Northern Thailand

Mountainous, with sharp curves and switchbacks. The roads are properly surfaced but the gradients and cornering are sustained rather than occasional.

Route 1095 between Chiang Mai and Pai is the specific stretch most often discussed. It is commonly cited as having 762 curves over roughly 135 km — a figure repeated on signage and in most accounts of the route, though it reads as a tourist landmark number rather than a survey measurement. What is not in dispute is the character: continuous mountain switchbacks, with limited lighting on the mountain sections.

Phuket

Hilly, with winding coastal and mountain roads connecting the west-coast beaches. Traffic volume is heavier than on the smaller islands, and the island is 48 to 50 km long, so distances between beaches involve real driving rather than short hops. Lighting on the connecting roads is limited.

Koh Samui

The ring road runs about 51 km around the island and is mostly flat coastal driving. The interior behind it is hilly, and the access roads climbing to interior viewpoints and resorts are steeper than the ring itself suggests. Lighting on the ring road is limited outside the built-up stretches.

The smaller southern islands

Mixed. Main roads are generally paved and in reasonable condition, and the surfacing has improved considerably in recent years. What varies is what happens off the main road.

On Koh Tao, one wide paved road connects Sairee, Mae Haad and Chalok Baan Kao, with side roads of similar quality running over to east-coast bays like Hin Wong, Tanote and Sai Daeng. Some dirt tracks remain in more remote areas, and some destinations need four-wheel drive to reach. The terrain between bays is hilly.

Koh Lanta is long and narrow with beaches along the west coast, and Koh Phangan spreads across multiple bays — in both cases the main coastal roads are paved, with the variation sitting in the access roads down to individual beaches.

Bangkok

Flat, dense, and the one place with reliably good street lighting in the urban core. Traffic volume rather than road surface is the governing condition.

Who shares the road

One characteristic that does not appear on a map: in the tourist areas, road users come from many countries with different driving conventions. Rules that are automatic in one place are unfamiliar in another, and the mix is at its most varied on the islands where rental vehicles are most common.

Roads are also shared with pedestrians and animals in the absence of footpaths, which is the practical reason the lighting question matters as much as it does.

How the physical picture fits the rest

Terrain, surfacing, traffic and lighting are inputs rather than answers. What they mean depends on how far you need to travel on any given day, what transport alternatives exist where you are staying, and whether the journeys in question happen in daylight.

How the road conditions combine with distances and transport coverage for a particular itinerary is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Are Thai roads well lit at night?

Outside Bangkok and the main urban areas, generally not. Island roads, mountain roads and rural stretches are largely unlit, and most island roads have no footpaths.

How difficult is the road from Chiang Mai to Pai?

It is continuous mountain driving — commonly cited as 762 curves over roughly 135 km, with sharp switchbacks and limited lighting on the mountain sections. The surface itself is properly made.

What are the roads like on Koh Tao?

One wide paved road connects the three main villages, with side roads of similar quality to the east-coast bays. Some dirt tracks remain in remote areas and some spots require four-wheel drive. The terrain between bays is hilly.

Is Phuket hilly?

Yes — winding coastal and mountain roads connect the west-coast beaches, and at 48 to 50 km long the distances between them involve real driving rather than short hops.

Do Thai island roads have sidewalks?

Mostly not. Walking between bays means sharing the carriageway with traffic, which matters most where lighting is absent after dark.
excerpt: Terrain, surfaces, traffic and lighting — the physical inputs, region by region.
